items.title: Babur & the Foundation of the Mughal Empire (1526-1530)
items.body:
## Babur — the founder

- **Zahiruddin Muhammad Babur** (b. 1483, Andijan, Ferghana) founded the Mughal Empire. He was a **descendant of Timur** (paternal) and **Genghis/Chinggis Khan** (maternal), inheriting the Timurid claim.
- After losing Samarqand and Ferghana in Central Asia, he captured **Kabul in 1504** and from there advanced on Hindustan.

## The four decisive battles

| Battle | Year | Opponent | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| **First Panipat** | 1526 | Ibrahim Lodi (Delhi Sultan) | Ended the Lodi/Delhi Sultanate; founded Mughal rule |
| **Khanwa** | 1527 | Rana Sanga (Mewar) | Broke Rajput confederacy; consolidated N. India |
| **Chanderi** | 1528 | Medini Rai (Malwa) | Captured Chanderi (Rajputs performed jauhar) |
| **Ghaghra** | 1529 | Afghan confederacy | Secured the east (Bihar/Bengal frontier) |

- At **Panipat** Babur, though outnumbered, used **field artillery** and the Ottoman (Rumi) **tulughma / linked-cart** tactic learnt from Chaldiran (1514).
- Babur wrote his memoirs, the **Baburnama (Tuzuk-i-Baburi)**, in **Chagatai Turkish** — a landmark autobiography. He introduced the **Charbagh** garden (Aram Bagh/Ram Bagh, Agra).
- Died at Agra in **1530**; succeeded by **Humayun**. His remains were later moved to **Bagh-e-Babur, Kabul**.
keyPoints: Babur, descendant of Timur and Genghis Khan, founded the Mughal Empire in 1526.
First Battle of Panipat (1526) defeated Ibrahim Lodi and ended the Delhi Sultanate.
Battle of Khanwa (1527) defeated Rana Sanga; Chanderi (1528) and Ghaghra (1529) followed.
Babur used artillery and the tulughma (linked-cart) tactic to beat larger armies.
He wrote the Baburnama (Tuzuk-i-Baburi) in Chagatai Turkish and introduced Charbagh gardens.
items.mnemonic: Babur's battles 'P-K-C-G' = Panipat, Khanwa, Chanderi, Ghaghra (1526-27-28-29).

items.title: Humayun & the Sur Interregnum (Sher Shah Suri)
items.body:
## Humayun (1530-40, 1555-56)

- Divided the empire among his brothers (**Kamran, Askari, Hindal**), weakening central control.
- Lost to the Afghan **Sher Shah Suri** at **Chausa (1539)** and **Kannauj/Bilgram (1540)**, then fled into **15 years of exile in Persia** (sheltered by **Shah Tahmasp** of the Safavids).
- **Recaptured Delhi in 1555** (battles of Machhiwara and Sirhind); died in **1556** after falling from his library stairs. His widow built **Humayun's Tomb** — India's **first garden tomb**, a model for the Taj Mahal.

## Sher Shah Suri (1540-45) — the great administrator

- Born **Farid Khan** in Sasaram (Bihar); earned the title **Sher Khan** for killing a tiger. Founded the **Sur dynasty** after defeating Humayun.
- **Revenue:** empire split into **sarkars → parganas**; land measured and classified; state share **one-third of produce**; peasants given **patta (title deed)** and **kabuliyat (agreement)**.
- **Economy & roads:** standardised the **silver rupiya and copper dam**; restored the **Grand Trunk Road** with **sarais (inns)** for travellers.
- **Military:** revived **dagh (branding of horses)** and **chehra (soldier descriptive roll)** from Alauddin Khalji.
- His reforms became the **base for Akbar's administration** and later British revenue systems; Humayun called him **'Ustad-i-Badshahan' (Teacher of Kings)**. Died at **Kalinjar (1545)** in a gunpowder blast.
keyPoints: Humayun lost to Sher Shah at Chausa (1539) and Kannauj (1540), then exiled to Safavid Persia.
He recaptured Delhi in 1555 and died in 1556; Humayun's Tomb is India's first garden tomb.
Sher Shah Suri (Farid Khan) founded the Sur dynasty and ruled 1540-45.
Sher Shah's revenue: sarkar/pargana units, one-third produce, patta and kabuliyat to peasants.
He introduced the silver rupiya and copper dam, revived the Grand Trunk Road with sarais, and used dagh & chehra.
items.mnemonic: Sher Shah = 'RRR' — Rupiya, Roads (GT Road), Revenue reforms.

items.title: Akbar the Great (1556-1605): Conquests, Religion & Administration
items.body:
## Accession & conquests

- **Jalal-ud-din Akbar** ascended at age 13 in **1556** under the regency of **Bairam Khan**, who won the **Second Battle of Panipat (1556)** against **Hemu**.
- Key campaigns: **Siege of Chittorgarh (1567-68)**, **Battle of Haldighati (1576)** against **Maharana Pratap** (Mughals led by **Man Singh**), annexation of **Gujarat (1573)** and **Bengal (1576)**.

## Religious policy

- Abolished the **jizya** on non-Muslims; promoted **Sulh-i-Kul (universal peace)** and interfaith dialogue at the **Ibadat Khana**.
- Founded the syncretic **Din-i-Ilahi** (1582), which won few followers.

## Administration

- **Dahsala / Zabti system** (with **Raja Todar Mal**) — revenue fixed on the **average produce & prices of 10 years**, state share one-third; also called **Todar Mal's Bandobast**. Alternatives: **Batai/Ghalla-Bakshi**, **Kankut**.
- **Mansabdari system** — every officer held a **mansab (rank)** with dual numbers, **Zat** (personal status/pay) and **Sawar** (cavalry to maintain); ranks ran 10 up to 5,000 (later 7,000 for princes).
- **Navaratnas (Nine Gems)** included **Todar Mal, Abul Fazl** (wrote **Akbarnama**, whose 3rd volume is the **Ain-i-Akbari**), **Tansen, Birbal, Raja Man Singh, Abdul Rahim Khan-i-Khanan, Faizi**.
keyPoints: Akbar acceded in 1556; Bairam Khan won the Second Battle of Panipat against Hemu.
Conquests: Chittorgarh (1567-68), Haldighati (1576) vs Maharana Pratap, Gujarat (1573), Bengal (1576).
Religious policy: abolished jizya, promoted Sulh-i-Kul, founded Din-i-Ilahi (1582).
Dahsala/Zabti (Todar Mal's Bandobast) fixed revenue on 10-year average produce, one-third share.
Mansabdari ranks had Zat (status) and Sawar (cavalry) components.
Abul Fazl wrote the Akbarnama; its third volume is the Ain-i-Akbari.

items.title: Jahangir & Shah Jahan: Nur Jahan, English Contact & the Architectural Peak
items.body:
## Jahangir (1605-1627)

- Prince **Salim** took the title **Jahangir ('world-seizer')**. Married **Mehr-un-Nisa (Nur Jahan)** in 1611, whose faction (the 'Nur Jahan Junta') dominated court.
- Famous for the **Zanjir-i-Adl (chain of justice)** at Agra Fort.
- **English contact:** Captain Hawkins visited; **Sir Thomas Roe** (envoy of James I) secured trading rights, and the English set up their **first factory at Surat (1613)**. Lost **Qandahar** to Persia (1622).

## Shah Jahan (1628-1658)

- Prince **Khurram**, titled **Shah Jahan**. Built the **Taj Mahal** for **Mumtaz Mahal (Arjumand Banu)**, who died in 1631.
- **Golden age of Mughal architecture:** Red Fort (Delhi), Jama Masjid, Moti Masjid, and the jewelled **Peacock Throne (Takht-i-Taus)**. Recovered **Qandahar (1638)** briefly; Balkh campaign.
- Fell ill in 1657, triggering the **war of succession** among his sons; **Aurangzeb** won and imprisoned him in **Agra Fort** until his death in **1666**.
keyPoints: Jahangir (Prince Salim) married Nur Jahan (1611), who wielded major political influence.
Sir Thomas Roe secured trading rights; the English set up their first factory at Surat in 1613.
Jahangir was known for the chain of justice (Zanjir-i-Adl) at Agra Fort.
Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal for Mumtaz Mahal and the Peacock Throne.
His reign is the golden age of Mughal architecture (Red Fort, Jama Masjid).
Aurangzeb won the war of succession and imprisoned Shah Jahan in Agra Fort till 1666.

items.title: Aurangzeb & the Decline of the Mughal Empire
items.body:
## Aurangzeb Alamgir (1658-1707)

- Won a **war of succession** against **Dara Shikoh**, imprisoned Shah Jahan, and ruled as **'Zinda Pir' (living saint)**, an orthodox Sunni.
- **Religious measures:** re-imposed **jizya in 1679**; appointed **muhtasibs (moral police)**; discontinued court music and the Nauroz festival; executed **Guru Tegh Bahadur (1675)**.
- **Deccan policy:** annexed **Bijapur and Golconda (1686-87)** — bringing Andhra's Qutb Shahi Golconda under Mughal rule — but decades of costly war against the **Marathas (Shivaji, Sambhaji)** drained the treasury.
- The empire reached its **greatest territorial extent** yet was fatally overstretched. He died at **Ahmednagar in 1707**.

## The Later Mughals & causes of decline

- Weak successors became **puppets of nobles** (Irani vs Turani factions); the **Sayyid Brothers** made and unmade emperors.
- **Nadir Shah of Persia** sacked Delhi in **1739** (**Battle of Karnal**) and carried off the **Peacock Throne and Koh-i-Noor**; **Ahmad Shah Abdali** raided five times (1748-61).
- Provinces broke away: **Hyderabad (Asaf Jahi/Nizam), Bengal (Murshid Quli Khan), Awadh**. The last emperor, **Bahadur Shah II**, was deposed after the **1857 Revolt** and exiled to Rangoon.
keyPoints: Aurangzeb won the war of succession against Dara Shikoh; called Zinda Pir.
He re-imposed jizya in 1679, appointed muhtasibs, and executed Guru Tegh Bahadur (1675).
Annexed Bijapur and Golconda (1686-87) but exhausted the empire in Deccan/Maratha wars; died 1707.
Nadir Shah sacked Delhi in 1739 (Battle of Karnal), taking the Peacock Throne and Koh-i-Noor.
Later Mughals were puppets of nobles like the Sayyid Brothers; provinces (Hyderabad, Bengal, Awadh) broke away.
Bahadur Shah II, the last Mughal, was exiled to Rangoon after the 1857 Revolt.
items.mnemonic: Aurangzeb = peak size but 'Deccan ulcer' + jizya (1679) = decline seed.

items.title: The Marathas: Shivaji & the Peshwas
items.body:
## Chhatrapati Shivaji (1630-1680)

- Born at **Shivneri Fort**; inspired by his mother **Jijabai** and guardian **Dadoji Kondadeo**. Coined **'Hindavi Swarajya'**.
- Rose against **Bijapur** — killed **Afzal Khan** at **Pratapgarh (1659)**; raided **Surat (1664)**; signed the **Treaty of Purandar (1665)** with Jai Singh; escaped Agra (1666).
- Crowned **Chhatrapati at Raigad in 1674**. Master of **guerrilla warfare** ('Mountain Rat'), he held **240-280 forts** and built a navy (Sindhudurg), earning 'Father of the Indian Navy'.
- **Ashtapradhan:** council of **eight ministers** (Peshwa, Amatya, etc.); promoted **Marathi/Sanskrit** in administration. Levied **Chauth** (1/4 of revenue) and **Sardeshmukhi** (additional 1/10) on neighbouring lands.

## The Peshwa era

- After Shivaji and **Sambhaji** (executed by Aurangzeb, 1689), **Shahu** appointed **Balaji Vishwanath** as **Peshwa (1713)** — power shifted to the Peshwas.
- **Baji Rao I** expanded into Malwa, Gujarat and Bundelkhand; **Balaji Baji Rao (Nana Saheb)** extended Maratha power till the disastrous **Third Battle of Panipat (1761)** loss to **Ahmad Shah Abdali**.
- The **Treaty of Salbai (1782)** ended the First Anglo-Maratha War.
keyPoints: Shivaji coined 'Hindavi Swarajya' and was crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad in 1674.
He killed Afzal Khan at Pratapgarh (1659), raided Surat (1664), and signed the Treaty of Purandar (1665).
Ashtapradhan was Shivaji's council of eight ministers headed by the Peshwa.
Chauth (1/4 of revenue) and Sardeshmukhi (extra 1/10) were the Maratha taxes.
Shahu made Balaji Vishwanath Peshwa in 1713, beginning the Peshwa era.
The Marathas lost the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) to Ahmad Shah Abdali.
